sections.h2: What is Upper Dublin Township like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Upper Dublin is a first-class township in Montgomery County, covering 13.3 square miles north of Philadelphia, with 26,665 residents at the 2020 census. It was farmland and limestone country until the 1950s, then filled in with postwar subdivisions: the population went from 6,637 in 1950 to 19,562 in 1970. Wikipedia ranks its median income fourth highest in the county.

The township's name goes back to a land grant that created Upper and Lower Dublin. Lower Dublin was folded into Philadelphia in 1854, and Upper Dublin kept going on its own, taking first-class township status on January 1, 1946. Limekiln Pike, a legacy of the township's limestone past, is still an important travel route.

Many addresses use a mailing name other than Upper Dublin. Those community areas include Ambler, Dresher, Fort Washington, Jarrettown and Maple Glen, with small slices of Abington, Ardsley, North Hills, Oreland and Willow Grove. They use ZIP codes 19001, 19002, 19025, 19034, 19038, 19075 and 19090, and none of them is a separate municipality. Property records and tax bills go through the township and county, regardless of the postal name.

sections.h2: How does the Fort Washington Office Park affect housing in Upper Dublin?
sections.html:
The office park is the township's economic engine. Wikipedia says it opened in 1955 as the first modern suburban business park on the East Coast, sits at a Pennsylvania Turnpike interchange, covers 566 acres and holds more than 80 buildings with over six million square feet of space. It is described as home to about 230 businesses and more than 12,000 workers.

The township has been planning for a change in mix, from light industrial toward offices, and has formed a municipal authority to finance public improvements there. A proposed mixed-use zoning change would allow more multifamily housing, retail and dining. For a seller in Maple Glen or Fort Washington, an employment hub a short drive away is an easy point to make in a listing.

  • Describe the commute to the office park and the turnpike interchange.
  • Note the Upper Dublin Public Library, which moved into a township-owned building in the park and opened in 2020.
  • Mention the township's seven wards if buyers ask who represents the street.

sections.h2: Did the 2021 tornado and flooding change anything for Upper Dublin sellers?
sections.html:
It left a record you may be asked about. An EF2 tornado spawned by the remnants of Hurricane Ida struck Upper Dublin on September 1, 2021, hitting the Fort Washington and Maple Glen areas. Nearly all of the township drains through Wissahickon Creek into the Schuylkill River, with only small corners draining to Neshaminy Creek and Pennypack Creek, so low lots near those streams deserve a closer look.

If your house had storm repairs, keep the permits, invoices and final inspection records together. Under the township's transfer process, every open permit must be closed out before the sale, so storm-era work that never received a final inspection is the kind of thing that stops a closing. The township's Code Enforcement department can tell you which permits on your address are still open.

Ask for a copy of the property file before you list. It also shows past zoning hearings tied to the address, which the township reviews at transfer.

sections.h2: What does Upper Dublin require before a property can be sold?
sections.html:
Upper Dublin has a point-of-sale process, and the township's Property Transfers page says every property being sold must submit a Property Transfer Application under Ordinance 10-1228. The steps run alongside your sale, so start early.

  • A township official inspects the exterior for sidewalk compliance and correct house numbering. Anything found must be fixed before the sale.
  • The property file is checked for open permits. Every open permit must be finalized before the sale.
  • The file is also reviewed for zoning hearings tied to the property.
  • You sign an affidavit that smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps are present.
  • Open Notices of Violation must be resolved before the sale.
  • Curbs and aprons are inspected and documented. The page says this is not required for the sale to proceed, but a failed curb or apron is marked for replacement under the property maintenance code.

Permits and applications go through the township's online OpenGov portal at upperdublin.net/permits. Paper applications are no longer available, so file everything there. Leave time for both the inspection and any sidewalk repair it turns up.

sections.h2: What does the Montgomery County transfer tax cost on an Upper Dublin sale?
sections.html:
Montgomery County's Recorder of Deeds states that the realty transfer tax is 2 percent. Pennsylvania's share is 1 percent, and the rest is local. The state says both parties to a deed are jointly responsible, so decide in the contract who pays. On a $500,000 sale, 2 percent comes to $10,000.

sections.h2: How do assessment appeals and delinquent taxes work in Upper Dublin?
sections.html:
Assessments are county business. The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals sets August 1 as the filing deadline for annual appeals, and the same date applies to exemption applications under 53 Pa.C.S. § 8844(c)(2). The county explains that annual appeals must be decided by October 31 so that new values reach taxing districts by November 15. Appeals are mailed to the Board at P.O. Box 311, Norristown, or hand-delivered during office hours.

Postmarks can lag. The county tells filers to ask for a hand cancellation, a certificate of mailing, registered or certified mail, or postage purchased at the counter. The Board's page also lists homestead forms, an exemption application and a "Taxing Authorities" document that names the school district and other taxing bodies for each address.

If you are behind on taxes, the Tax Claim Bureau holds an upset sale each September and December of parcels whose taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid. Buyers at an upset sale take on all liens, and the Bureau advertises each property beforehand. Paying the delinquent bill first, or selling before your parcel is listed, keeps the house out of that sale.

sections.h2: What are my options if I need to sell an Upper Dublin house fast?
sections.html:
You can list, sell privately, or take a cash offer from a buyer who buys houses as-is. The township's transfer requirements apply to each route, so the real question is who finishes the paperwork and how soon.

  • List when open permits are closed, the sidewalk is sound and the house shows well.
  • Choose a cash sale when you inherited the house, face repairs, or have a closing date to meet. Confirm the buyer will handle the sidewalk, permit and affidavit steps with you.

Whichever route you choose, call Code Enforcement first, get the property file, and make sure the 2 percent transfer tax is set out in writing.

faqs.q: Does Upper Dublin require an inspection to sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. Every property sold must file a Property Transfer Application, and a township official inspects the exterior for sidewalks and house numbers. Open permits and open violations must be cleared before the sale, and you sign an affidavit about smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps.

faqs.q: What is the transfer tax in Upper Dublin?
faqs.a: The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds lists the realty transfer tax at 2 percent, which includes the state's 1 percent. Both buyer and seller are liable under state law, so the sales contract should say who pays.

faqs.q: When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: August 1 each year for annual appeals. The same deadline applies to exemption applications, and the Board advises hand delivery or a post office counter postmark.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Upper Dublin house that has open permits?
faqs.a: Not until the permits are finalized. The township's transfer review checks the property file, and every open permit must be closed before the sale, so schedule the missing inspections first.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay my property taxes before selling?
faqs.a: Unpaid taxes become a lien and can lead to a Tax Claim Bureau sale. The Bureau runs an upset sale each September and December for parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier, and buyers there take on the liens.
